question: Why should only Shell call history.pushState(), and not the MFEs themselves?

options.text: Because MFEs are loaded lazily and do not have access to window.history until fully initialized
options.explanation: Lazy loading does not restrict access to window.history — after mounting, an MFE has full access to the browser API. The issue is not availability, but coordination.

options.text: Because two MFEs can call pushState simultaneously; the second call silently overwrites the first — the URL becomes incorrect and MFE states become desynchronized
options.explanation: history.pushState() does not emit events and does not throw exceptions on conflict. In a race condition both calls will execute, but only the last URL will remain in the browser — this leads to an inconsistent application state.

options.text: Because React Router in an MFE cannot work with the native history API — only through its own abstractions
options.explanation: React Router uses the history API internally — it works with it perfectly. The restriction is an architectural decision for coordination, not a technical limitation of React Router.

options.text: Because the browser blocks pushState calls from iframes, and MFEs often use iframe isolation
options.explanation: Not all MFEs use iframes. With iframes history is indeed isolated, but the question is about the more general case — JS integration where all MFEs share the same window.

question: Shell declares the route `/catalog/*`. What internal routes configuration should Catalog MFE use?

options.text: <Route path="/catalog" />, <Route path="/catalog/search" />, <Route path="/catalog/:id" />
options.explanation: Duplicating the /catalog prefix in the MFE's internal routes is a common mistake. React Router already knows the MFE handles paths under /catalog/* — so only relative paths are needed inside.

options.text: <Route index />, <Route path="search" />, <Route path=":id" />
options.explanation: Inside a Route with path='/catalog/*', React Router v6 automatically knows the base path. Relative paths (search, :id, index) correctly resolve to /catalog/search and /catalog/:id — without duplicating the prefix.

options.text: <Route path="/*" />, <Route path="/*/search" />, <Route path="/*/:id" />
options.explanation: This syntax is not a valid way to write relative routes in React Router v6. A wildcard as a path segment placeholder does not work this way.

options.text: Catalog MFE should not have its own Router — Shell fully manages all routes
options.explanation: Shell manages only the top level (/catalog/*). Internal routes are the responsibility of Catalog MFE. This is the key principle of nested routing in MFEs: Shell delegates internal navigation to the MFE.

question: A user enters the URL `/catalog/42` directly into the browser address bar. What should the server do?

options.text: Return 404 — the server does not know about /catalog/42, it is an SPA route
options.explanation: Returning 404 breaks deep linking — one of the key features of modern applications. Users will not be able to share links to specific pages.

options.text: Perform server-side rendering of Catalog MFE with ProductDetail for ID 42
options.explanation: SSR is one possible approach, but not the only one or a required one. For most internal applications, client-side deep linking with proper nginx configuration is sufficient.

options.text: Return index.html for any path that is not a static file — the SPA will handle the URL itself
options.explanation: The try_files $uri /index.html pattern in nginx is the standard solution for SPA deep linking. Shell loads, sees the URL /catalog/42, determines the appropriate MFE, and mounts it with initialPath='/catalog/42'.

options.text: Redirect to / via a 302 redirect — the user will navigate to the needed page themselves
options.explanation: Redirecting to / destroys the deep link — the user loses context. This is an anti-pattern that makes it impossible to share links to specific pages of the application.

question: A developer places a wildcard route `*` first in the Shell routes list. What will happen?

options.text: Nothing special — React Router v6 automatically sorts routes by specificity
options.explanation: React Router v6 does use a ranking algorithm for most routes, but wildcard (*) is still order-sensitive in some scenarios. Best practice is to always place * last.

options.text: The wildcard will intercept all requests — the specific routes /catalog/*, /cart/* will never match
options.explanation: The * route matches any path. If it is first, the router will stop at it and never check more specific routes. Wildcard must always be last — this is not just style, it is correctness.

options.text: React Router will throw a compile error — a wildcard cannot appear before other routes
options.explanation: React Router does not throw an error for this ordering — it is a logical configuration mistake that must be caught through tests or config validation.

options.text: The wildcard will only be used if no other route matched — order does not matter
options.explanation: In most routers, order matters. In React Router v6, the ranking algorithm helps for regular routes, but for wildcard — it is safer to explicitly place it last.

question: What mechanism is best suited for passing a navigation request from Cart MFE to Shell?

options.text: CustomEvent on window with the name 'mfe:navigate' and detail.path
options.explanation: Custom Events are a native browser standard. No additional dependencies are needed; they work between any MFEs without a shared library and are easy to debug in DevTools.

options.text: Shared Navigation Bus — a singleton in a shared package, Shell subscribes via onNavigate()
options.explanation: A Navigation Bus provides additional capabilities: guards (auth check, unsaved changes), middleware, centralized logging. Suitable for applications with complex navigation requirements.

options.text: Direct call to window.history.pushState() from Cart MFE
options.explanation: This is exactly what should not be done. Calling pushState directly from an MFE bypasses the Shell router, creates a risk of race conditions, and makes centralized auth guards or navigation analytics impossible.

options.text: localStorage.setItem('navigate', path) + window 'storage' event
options.explanation: Using localStorage to coordinate navigation is an anti-pattern. localStorage is asynchronous (storage events do not guarantee order), pollutes the store, and complicates debugging. Specialized mechanisms exist for navigation.

question: Shell loads Catalog MFE with `path='/catalog/*'`. The user opens a deep link `/catalog/42`. How should Catalog MFE handle the initial URL?

options.text: Catalog MFE always starts at / — the user must navigate manually
options.explanation: Ignoring initialPath breaks deep linking. A user who opened /catalog/42 from a bookmark or an email expects to see product card 42, not the catalog list.

options.text: Catalog MFE reads window.location.pathname and extracts the path, passing it to MemoryRouter via initialEntries or to BrowserRouter via the built-in match
options.explanation: On mount, the MFE must initialize its internal router with the current pathname. This allows the correct view (ProductDetail for /catalog/42) to be shown on a direct URL navigation.

options.text: Shell intercepts /catalog/42 and renders ProductDetail itself without Catalog MFE — it is faster
options.explanation: Shell should not know about Catalog MFE's internal components. This violates encapsulation and creates tight coupling — Shell becomes dependent on the implementation details of each MFE.

options.text: Catalog MFE redirects to /catalog and then does a client-side navigate to /catalog/42
options.explanation: The extra redirect /catalog → /catalog/42 creates an artifact in the browser history and an unpleasant UI flash. The correct approach is to immediately initialize the router with the correct path.

question: What is the difference between lazy and eager loading of MFEs in Shell route configuration?

options.text: A lazy MFE loads only on the first visit to its route — reduces Shell's initial bundle size
options.explanation: Lazy loading via dynamic import() defers loading the MFE until the user navigates to its route. Shell starts faster by not loading all MFE code upfront.

options.text: An eager MFE is included in the Shell's main bundle — available instantly, but increases page load time
options.explanation: Eager loading means Shell imports the MFE statically. There is no additional network request when navigating to the route, but Shell takes longer to load due to the larger bundle.

options.text: A lazy MFE does not support deep linking — a direct visit to /catalog/42 with a lazy Catalog MFE will cause an error
options.explanation: Lazy MFEs support deep linking perfectly. On a direct visit to /catalog/42, Shell loads the lazy Catalog MFE (a small delay) and passes it the initialPath. Suspense provides a fallback while loading.

options.text: A lazy MFE must be wrapped in Suspense with a fallback to handle the loading state
options.explanation: React lazy() combined with dynamic import() throws a Promise on first load — this is the Suspense mechanism. Without <Suspense fallback={...}>, React will throw an error. The fallback shows a skeleton or spinner while the MFE is loading.

question: A team proposes using hash-routing (#/catalog/42) instead of the history API to avoid conflicts. What are the consequences?

options.text: Hash routing is not sent to the server — nginx does not need to be configured, deep links work out of the box
options.explanation: The hash part of the URL (#/catalog/42) is not included in the HTTP request. The server always receives a request for /, returns index.html, and the SPA handles the hash on the client — no special nginx configuration needed.

options.text: Hash routing is worse for SEO — search engines have historically ignored or poorly indexed hash paths
options.explanation: Google has learned to index JavaScript applications, but hash URLs are still considered an anti-pattern for SEO. For public-facing sites, history API + SSR or prerendering is preferable.

options.text: Hash routing completely solves the pushState conflict problem — conflicts become impossible
options.explanation: Hash routing replaces pushState with location.hash changes, but race conditions do not go away. Two MFEs can simultaneously change location.hash — the coordination problem remains.

options.text: The URL looks less professional: http://app.com/#/catalog/42 instead of http://app.com/catalog/42
options.explanation: Hash URLs look different and are perceived as an outdated approach. For corporate and public-facing applications this can be an important factor.

question: A navigation guard in Shell must check authorization before transitioning to protected routes. Where is the best place to put this logic?

options.text: In each MFE separately — they check the token themselves before rendering their components
options.explanation: Duplicating auth logic in every MFE violates DRY and creates a risk of desynchronization. If the authorization logic changes, all MFEs need to be updated simultaneously. A single authorization point is easier to maintain.

options.text: In the mfe:navigate event handler in Shell, before calling router.navigate()
options.explanation: A centralized guard in Shell is the correct architectural solution. Shell intercepts all navigation requests, checks permissions before the transition, and only on success calls router.navigate(). All MFEs are automatically protected.

options.text: In the React Router loader function in the Shell routes configuration
options.explanation: A loader is a good option for data-fetching, but for a navigation guard an interceptor at the navigation level is preferable. The loader runs after the transition has already begun, which can lead to a flash of unprotected content.

options.text: In a shared AuthService that MFEs call independently before each user action
options.explanation: AuthService in every MFE duplicates integration points. If an MFE calls navigate() through Shell, then authorization checks should also be in Shell — a single entry point for all navigation.

question: A project uses Module Federation. Shell and Catalog MFE both include react-router-dom in shared with singleton:true. What will happen with browser history?

options.text: Each MFE will have its own independent navigation history — a pushState in one is not visible to the other
options.explanation: This describes behavior with a NON-shared router. With singleton:true both MFEs use one copy of react-router-dom — and one RouterContext. Browser history is shared.

options.text: Both use a single react-router-dom instance — they share one RouterContext and one history
options.explanation: Singleton means one copy in the runtime. Shell creates a BrowserRouter (or createBrowserRouter), Catalog MFE gets access to the same RouterContext through shared react-router-dom. useNavigate() in Catalog works with the same history.

options.text: Module Federation will throw an error — react-router-dom does not support singleton mode
options.explanation: react-router-dom works perfectly as a singleton in Module Federation. Moreover, this is the recommended approach — without singleton, two routers compete for the same browser history.

options.text: Shell will use the current version, Catalog MFE — a cached old copy
options.explanation: Singleton guarantees one version for all. Module Federation performs version negotiation and loads the maximum compatible version — not 'current for one' and 'cached for another'.
